clauses.reason: Terminated on 1934-09-14, the date the order issued: the clause only terminates a stay ('do hereby order that the stay of the provisions of Section 1 of Article IX of such Code be terminated'), a one-time act that commands nothing afterwards and is exhausted by performance on its own date. Actor: EO 6847-A itself; the cited text is the order's own operative sentence. The code provision that the termination released, Section 1 of Article IX, operated only through the code, whose approval and enforcement ended with the repeal on 1935-06-14 under section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 ('All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed'); that repeal is recorded as a later event of the code, not as the end of this exhausted clause, and the surviving consequence is not a continuing command of this order. Schechter (1935-05-27) is a validity characterization of the section 3 delegation, not an end date for this order.

Terminated by statute on June 14, 1935. The clause provides that 'Except as provided herein, the provisions of the Executive Order of June 9, 1934, approving such Code, shall remain in full force and effect'; it preserves the approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Wheat Flour Milling Industry (and the earlier order's other stays and conditions) and can end no later than the approval it preserves. Actor: Congress, S.J. Res. 113, section 2, approved June 14, 1935. Legal basis for the first end. An approval of a code under section 3 of title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act had legal effect only through section 3: under 3(b) the code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry and a violation in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and district attorneys were directed to sue, and under 3(f) each violation was a misdemeanor (the section 3 excerpt held in this packet). Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935 (49 Stat. 375), repealed 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes' and states no effective date other than its approval. That repeal removed the power the approval rested on and every provision through which the approved code was enforced, which is the reason (not a default date) that it ends the prospective operative effect of this command on June 14, 1935. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495 (decided May 27, 1935), held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional ('we hold the code provisions here in question to be invalid'); the held excerpts record that as a validity characterization (an approval under an unconstitutional delegation was void from issuance under the doctrine then prevailing, and May 27, 1935 is when that was declared), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no other approving order and a later doctrine treats a measure's earlier existence as an operative fact. June 16, 1935 is not an end: section 1 of the resolution replaced the two-year expiry in section 2(c) with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935; EO 6999 (March 30, 1935) transfers the Secretary of Agriculture's functions under the code to the National Industrial Recovery Board and cancels nothing.

research_rationale:
EO 6847-A (September 14, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) terminates the stay of Section 1 of Article IX of the Code of Fair Competition for the Wheat Flour Milling Industry, which the order of June 9, 1934 approving the code had imposed, and states that the rest of that approving order remains in force. The held text has three 'Whereas' recitals (the June 9, 1934 approval; the approving order's stay of Article IX 'until such time as the Secretary of Agriculture determines and declares in writing, after adequate investigation, that an emergency exists'; and the facts presented by members of the industry) and one operative sentence pair beginning 'Now, therefore'. The machine inventory is one clause spanning the whole text including the recitals; I replaced it with two clauses (inventory correction recorded): clause 1, characters 753 to 1059, the command that the stay of Section 1 of Article IX 'be terminated'; clause 2, characters 1060 to 1201, 'Except as provided herein, the provisions of the Executive Order of June 9, 1934, approving such Code, shall remain in full force and effect.' Clause 1 is a one-time act exhausted by performance on the order's own date (the shared analysis treats such one-time determinations the same way: the command is exhausted on its date and the repeal is a later event); clause 2 preserves the June 9, 1934 order's provisions, so it can end no later than the approval it preserves, which ended June 14, 1935 by the repeal. The recital's own-terms wording ('until such time as the Secretary of Agriculture determines...') describes the earlier order's stay and is not a term of this order's commands. savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the Wheat Flour Milling code, including under Section 1 of Article IX after the stay of it was terminated on September 14, 1934, and before June 14, 1935 are completed (accrued) effects; the general savings statute of the time, which ordinarily preserves liabilities incurred under a repealed statute, is not a held source, and the repeal text contains no savings clause. Section 5 of title I exempted from the antitrust laws any code approved and in effect under the title and any action complying with it taken during the period; the resolution's proviso limits that exemption to agreements and action thereunder of two stated kinds and states no time limit, so the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action taken under codes before June 14, 1935. Whatever exemption or liability survives for past action is an accrued effect of completed acts, not continued operation of this order. The termination of the stay is a performed act: its consequence (Section 1 of Article IX no longer stayed) was a consequence for the code's operation, which ended June 14, 1935, and is not a surviving command of this order. No held source shows a proceeding under the code continuing after June 14, 1935.
